What is a tag question?

Great question! A tag question is a short question we add to the end of a sentence to check or confirm something. For example: 'You are in Primary 4, aren't you?' The first part is a statement, and the little question at the end is the tag. We use tag questions all the time when we speak: 'It is hot today, isn't it?' 'Bola can sing, can't she?' The tag invites the other person to agree or answer. Listen out for tag questions when people around you talk. You will hear them everywhere!

What is the rule for forming tag questions?

Well done for asking! The main rule is simple: a positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. For example: 'Ngozi is your friend, isn't she?' The statement is positive, so the tag 'isn't she' is negative. But 'Ngozi is not here, is she?' has a negative statement, so the tag 'is she' is positive. The tag also uses the same helping verb as the sentence, and a pronoun like he, she, it or they. Think of it like a see-saw: when one side goes up, the other goes down!

What is the tag question for 'You can swim'?

Let us work it out! The sentence 'You can swim' is positive, so the tag must be negative. The helping verb is 'can', so the tag uses 'can't'. The pronoun stays 'you'. Putting it together: 'You can swim, can't you?' Notice the comma before the tag and the question mark at the end. Here are similar ones: 'Tunde can draw, can't he?' and 'They can dance, can't they?' The pattern is always the same: repeat the helping verb, flip it, add the pronoun. Try making one with 'She can cook.' Excellent work!

How do I make a tag question when the sentence has no helping verb, like 'Ada likes rice'?

Very good question! When a sentence has no helping verb, we borrow 'do', 'does' or 'did' for the tag. 'Ada likes rice' is present tense with 'she', so we use 'doesn't': 'Ada likes rice, doesn't she?' For 'They play football', we say: 'They play football, don't they?' For the past tense, 'Musa went to Abuja', we use 'didn't': 'Musa went to Abuja, didn't he?' So do, does and did are helpers we call on when no other helping verb is in the sentence. Practise with 'Papa drinks tea.' You are doing brilliantly!

What is the tag question for 'It is not raining'?

Good one! The sentence 'It is not raining' is negative because of the word 'not'. So the tag must be positive. The helping verb is 'is' and the pronoun is 'it'. The answer is: 'It is not raining, is it?' Notice we do not say 'isn't it' here, because the sentence is already negative and two negatives would break the see-saw rule. More examples: 'You are not tired, are you?' and 'Chika does not like noise, does she?' Negative sentence, positive tag, every time. You have got this!

Why do we use tag questions when we speak?

Lovely question! We use tag questions for three main reasons.

First, to confirm something we think is true: 'The test is on Monday, isn't it?'
Second, to invite someone to agree with us: 'The jollof rice is delicious, isn't it?'
Third, to start a friendly conversation politely: 'You are new in this school, aren't you?' Tag questions make our speech warm and polite instead of blunt. Nigerians use them every day in the market, at home and in school. Use one politely today and see how friendly it sounds!

Complete this sentence with the correct tag: 'Your parents will come to the open day, ...?'

Let us solve it together! The statement 'Your parents will come to the open day' is positive, so the tag must be negative. The helping verb is 'will', and its negative is 'won't'. 'Your parents' becomes the pronoun 'they'. So the full sentence is: 'Your parents will come to the open day, won't they?' Remember the three steps: find the helping verb, flip positive to negative, and change the subject to a pronoun. Try this one yourself: 'Amina will win the prize, ...?' Well done, you are mastering tags!

Is 'isn't it' correct for every sentence, like some people say?

What a sharp observation! No, 'isn't it' does not fit every sentence, even though we often hear people use it that way. The tag must match the helping verb and the subject of the sentence. We say 'She is tall, isn't she?' but 'They are tall, aren't they?' and 'He can drive, can't he?' Using 'isn't it' everywhere, like 'They have gone, isn't it?', is a common error; the correct tag is 'haven't they?' Now you know the rule, you can speak better English than many adults. Keep listening carefully!
